content: Treatment for active (symptomatic) multiple myeloma typically involves pharmacological regimens that include steroid therapy, immune modulator therapy, and chemotherapy. In contrast, patients with smoldering (asymptomatic) multiple myeloma are managed through observation and regular follow-up tests every 3 to 6 months. The choice of optimal therapy for active multiple myeloma depends on whether the patient is eligible for bone marrow transplantation. For patients eligible for bone marrow transplantation, pharmacological treatment options include dexamethasone, lenalidomide, bortezomib, thalidomide, carfilzomib, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, or doxorubicin. For patients who are not eligible for transplantation, treatment regimens may include melphalan or prednisone. Alkylating agents are not recommended for transplant-eligible patients due to their toxicity, which can complicate the harvesting of bone marrow stem cells later in the disease course. Smoldering Multiple Myeloma Patients with smoldering multiple myeloma are managed through observation and follow-up tests every 3 to 6 months. These follow-up tests include: Laboratory studies such as complete blood count, electrolytes, 24-hour urine collection, electrophoresis, and quantitative immunoglobulin analysis. Imaging studies such as skeletal surveys, MRI, and PET scans. Flow cytometry and bone marrow aspiration/biopsy as needed. Treatment is deferred until symptoms develop. Active Multiple Myeloma The choice of therapy for active multiple myeloma depends on the patient’s eligibility for bone marrow transplantation. Key factors influencing transplant eligibility include: Type of chromosomal mutation. Age. Presence of associated diseases. Liver function. Kidney function. Initial Therapy Preferred pharmacological regimens for transplant-eligible patients include: Bortezomib/dexamethasone. Bortezomib/dexamethasone/lenalidomide. Dexamethasone/lenalidomide. Bortezomib/dexamethasone/doxorubicin. Bortezomib/dexamethasone/thalidomide. Bortezomib/dexamethasone/cyclophosphamide. For transplant-ineligible patients, preferred regimens include: Bortezomib/dexamethasone. Low-dose dexamethasone/lenalidomide. Melphalan/prednisone/thalidomide. Melphalan/prednisone/bortezomib. The VAD regimen (vincristine, adriamycin, and dexamethasone) has shown efficacy rates of 60–80% in both previously treated and untreated patients. This regimen avoids early exposure to alkylating agents, reducing the risks of myelosuppression and secondary leukemias without compromising efficacy. One commonly used induction regimen includes dexamethasone with lenalidomide and bortezomib for a period of 8 months, tailored based on side effect profiles and associated comorbidities. Lenalidomide is administered orally but increases the risk of deep vein thrombosis, while bortezomib is given intravenously and is preferred in patients with abnormal renal function. Dexamethasone alone, at a dose of 40 mg for 4 consecutive days, has shown efficacy comparable to the VAD combination. Thalidomide has been evaluated in multiple trials as an independent induction agent, demonstrating improved response rates without reducing stem cell load. Alkylating agents, such as melphalan and oral cyclophosphamide combined with prednisolone, are equally effective when used with VAD regimens. Supportive Therapy Supportive therapy is tailored to the patient’s symptoms and the side effects of medications. It includes: Bisphosphonates to prevent osteoporosis. Erythropoietin to prevent anemia. Vaccines to prevent recurrent infections. Blood thinners to prevent blood clots. Plasmapheresis to prevent hyperviscosity and renal failure. Maintenance Therapy After several months of induction therapy, the benefits of continuing the same therapy diminish. Maintenance therapy with newer agents such as thalidomide, lenalidomide, or bortezomib is often initiated. However, further clinical trials are needed to establish the efficacy of these agents in the maintenance phase.
